paraphrase: I praise Agni, the household priest (purohita), the god of the sacrifice, the officiant (ṛtvij), the invoker (hotṛ), best bestower of treasure.

Agni rules over the sacrifices as the shining guardian of ṛta, growing in his own home; the singer asks him to be easy of approach 'as a father to his son' and to stay with us for our well-being.
The wise (sūri) ever see that highest step of Viṣṇu, like an eye stretched out in heaven.

Varuṇa, of firm ordinances, knows the track of the birds through the air, the ships on the sea, the twelve months and the thirteenth that is born, the path of the wind; seated in his dwellings for universal rule, he beholds all wonders, what has been done and what is to be done.
The seer proclaims the heroic deeds of Indra, the first he did with the mace: he slew the serpent (ahi), bored out the waters and split the bellies of the mountains.

paraphrase: Rudra is praised as lord of songs, lord of the sacrifice, possessing the healing jalāṣa remedy; from him we ask the favour of Śaṃyu.
Looking up from the darkness to the higher light, we have come to Sūrya, god among the gods, the highest light.

paraphrase: May auspicious intentions (kratu) come to us from every side, undeceived, unhindered, breaking through, so that the gods may always be for our increase, unceasing guardians day by day.

paraphrase: Gods, may we hear with our ears what is auspicious; worshipful ones, may we see with our eyes what is auspicious; with firm limbs and bodies, praising you, may we attain the life-span set by the gods.

paraphrase: May Mitra, Varuṇa, Aryaman, Indra, Bṛhaspati and wide-striding Viṣṇu be propitious (śam) to us.
notes: Also the opening peace invocation of the Taittirīya Upaniṣad (reference only).

paraphrase: Mortals who saw the earlier dawn shining forth have gone; she is now seen by us; they too come who will see her in later days.
Rudra is asked not to harm our children and grandchildren, our life, our cows and horses, nor to slay our heroes in anger; with oblations we ever call on him.
notes: This verse recurs in the Śatarudrīya (TS 4.5.10; VS 16.16), reference from memory for the exact positions.

paraphrase: The bright face of the gods has risen, the eye of Mitra, Varuṇa and Agni; Sūrya has filled heaven, earth and the atmosphere — Sūrya is the self (ātman) of what moves and what stands.

Viṣṇu measured out the earthly realms and propped up the upper abode with three strides; in his three steps all beings dwell; the seer longs to reach his dear abode, where god-seeking men rejoice — for in Viṣṇu's highest step is a well-spring of honey (madhva utsaḥ).
notes: 1.154.5 contains 'viṣṇoḥ pade parame madhva utsaḥ' (checked).

paraphrase: Addressed to the sacrificial horse: 'you do not really die, nor are you harmed; you go to the gods by easy paths'.
Of this lovely grey hotṛ there is a middle brother, the eater (lightning or wind); the third brother has ghee on his back; here I saw the lord of the clans with seven sons.
notes: The identifications (Agni/sun, wind/lightning, earthly fire) are the commentators', not the verse's.

paraphrase: Seven yoke the one-wheeled chariot; one horse with seven names draws it; the wheel has three naves, is unaging and unassailable, and on it all these worlds rest.
Who has seen the first-born, when the boneless bore the one with bones? Where was the breath (asu), the blood, the self (ātman) of the earth? Who went to one who knows to ask this?
Not knowing, I ask the seers who know, as one who does not know, for the sake of knowing: what was the One, in the form of the unborn, that propped apart these six regions?
The twelve-spoked wheel of ṛta rolls around heaven and never wears out; on it, Agni, stand seven hundred and twenty sons in pairs.
notes: The tradition reads the twelve spokes as months and the 720 sons as the days and nights of the year.

paraphrase: Two birds, companions joined together, embrace the same tree; one of them eats the sweet fig, the other, not eating, looks on.

The living one moves by the self-powers (svadhā) of the dead; the immortal is of one origin with the mortal.
I saw the herdsman who never rests, going to and fro on the paths; clothed in the converging and diverging (regions) he keeps revolving within the worlds.
notes: Repeated as RV 10.177.3; the herdsman is read by the commentators as the sun, and by some later interpreters as the life-breath (interpretive).

paraphrase: He who made him does not know him; from him who saw him he is hidden; enveloped within his mother's womb, having many offspring (bahuprajāḥ), he has entered Nirṛti.
notes: Nirukta 2.8 records two readings of this verse: the wandering ascetics' (many births → misery) and the etymologists' (rain).

paraphrase: I do not know what I am like; secret, bound up, I wander with my mind; when the first-born of ṛta came to me, then I obtained a share of this speech.

original.edition: Śākala Saṃhitā, standard text (IAST, accents omitted); wording checked against the Devanāgarī text in sources_raw/DharmicData

paraphrase: Downward and upward goes the immortal, held by its own power (svadhā), of one origin with the mortal; the two go on for ever in opposite directions; people perceive the one and do not perceive the other.
The verses (ṛc) rest on the syllable (akṣara) in the highest heaven, on which all the gods have sat down; what will one who does not know that do with the verse? Those who know it sit here together.

paraphrase: The buffalo-cow (Gaurī) lowed, fashioning the waters: one-footed, two-footed, four-footed, eight-footed, nine-footed, she became thousand-syllabled in the highest heaven; from her the oceans flow out in all directions, from that the syllable flows, on which all the world lives.
notes: The Anukramaṇī gives the deity of the first half of verse 42 as Vāc and of the second as the Waters.

paraphrase: Speech is measured in four quarters (pada); the brahmins who are wise know them; three, placed in secret, do not stir; men speak the fourth quarter of speech.

paraphrase: They call it Indra, Mitra, Varuṇa, Agni, and it is the heavenly, fair-winged Garutmant; the One Being the inspired speak of in many ways — they call it Agni, Yama, Mātariśvan.

original.edition: Śākala Saṃhitā, standard text (IAST, accents omitted); wording checked against the Devanāgarī text in sources_raw/DharmicData

notes: The first principle of this ontology (config/principles.md). The Anukramaṇī gives the deity of 46–47 as Sūrya.

paraphrase: Twelve fellies, one wheel, three naves — who has understood it? In it are set together three hundred and sixty (spokes) like pegs that do not waver.
notes: The Anukramaṇī names its deity 'the year, the wheel of time' (saṃvatsara kālacakra).

paraphrase: With the sacrifice the gods sacrificed to the sacrifice; these were the first ordinances (dharma); those powers reached the vault of heaven where the ancient Sādhya gods are.
notes: Identical with RV 10.90.16.

paraphrase: Dialogue of Lopāmudrā and Agastya: she, worn by many autumns of toil, says old age wears away the beauty of bodies and that even the ancient truth-keeping seers who spoke truths with the gods ceased without reaching the end; he answers that toil guarded by the gods is not in vain and that the two together will win; his pupil asks forgiveness for any fault, since 'a mortal is full of desires'; the fierce seer Agastya, digging with spades, desiring offspring and strength, nourished both 'colours' (ubhau varṇau) and his wishes came true among the gods.
speaker: Lopāmudrā (1–2), Agastya (3–4), Agastya's pupil (5–6)
notes: Speaker division from the Anukramaṇī (checked). What 'both colours' means (tapas and progeny; or two classes) is left to the commentators.

paraphrase: The terrible one of whom they ask 'where is he?', of whom they say 'he does not exist' — he diminishes the enemy's wealth like stakes in a game; have faith (śrad dhatta) in him: he, O people, is Indra.
notes: One of the earliest recorded doubts about a god's existence, met with a call to faith (cf. 8.100.3–4).

paraphrase: Varuṇa is asked to loosen sin (āgas) from me like a rope, so that we may prosper at the spring of ṛta; may the thread not be cut while I weave my thought (dhī), nor the measure of the work break before its time.
notes: Seer: Kūrma Gārtsamada or Gṛtsamada; verse 10 of this hymn is marked against bad dreams.

paraphrase: With the most wholesome remedies given by you, Rudra, may I attain a hundred winters; drive hatred, distress (aṃhas) and diseases far from us in every direction.
May we not anger you, Rudra, with our homage, bad praise or joint invocation; raise up our heroes with remedies — I hear that you are the best physician of physicians.
Where, Rudra, is your gracious hand, the healing, cooling (jalāṣa) one that removes divinely-caused harm? Bull, have mercy on me.
Worthy, you bear arrows and bow; worthy, the adorable necklace of every form; worthy, you protect this whole vast world — there is nothing mightier than you, Rudra.
Three thousand three hundred and thirty-nine gods have worshipped Agni, anointed him with ghee, strewn grass for him and seated him as hotṛ.

Dialogue of Viśvāmitra with the rivers Vipāś and Śutudrī: the seer, wishing to cross with the Bharatas, asks them to stop; the rivers, who speak as seers in their own verses, first answer that they flow by Indra's command, then yield to the seer's words and lower their waters.
notes: The Anukramaṇī counts the rivers as ṛṣikās of verses 4, 6, 8, 10 (checked).

paraphrase: Imprecation verses (abhiśāpa) at the end of a hymn of Viśvāmitra against those who hate us; the tradition holds that they are directed at Vasiṣṭha, and Vasiṣṭha's descendants do not recite or hear them.
notes: The verses themselves do not name Vasiṣṭha; the attribution and the recitation custom are the tradition's (commentarial) account, recalled with moderate confidence.

paraphrase: Refrain of the hymn: 'great is the one lordship (asuratva) of the gods' (mahad devānām asuratvam ekam), repeated in each of its twenty-two verses on the dawns, fires and powers.
notes: Seer: Prajāpati Vaiśvāmitra or Prajāpati Vācya (Anukramaṇī, checked).

paraphrase: We meditate on that excellent radiance of the god Savitṛ; may he impel our thoughts (dhī).

paraphrase: While still in the womb I knew all the births of the gods; a hundred iron fortresses guarded me, then as a falcon I swiftly flew out.

paraphrase: The swan (haṃsa) seated in the bright, the good one in the atmosphere, the hotṛ at the altar, the guest in the house; seated in men, in the choicest, in ṛta, in the sky; born of waters, of cows, of ṛta, of the rock — ṛta (itself).
notes: Deity Sūrya (Anukramaṇī, checked). Quoted in the Kaṭha Upaniṣad (2.2.2) of the one who dwells in all (reference only).

paraphrase: From the ocean the honeyed wave arose; with the soma-stalk it attained immortality; the secret name of ghee is 'tongue of the gods', 'navel of immortality'.
notes: Deity: Agni, Sūrya, the waters, the cows, or praise of ghee (Anukramaṇī, checked).

paraphrase: Four horns, three feet, two heads, seven hands has he; the bull, bound threefold, roars; the great god has entered mortals.

paraphrase: Viśvavārā, facing east with the ladle, offers to the gods as Agni, kindled, sends his light to heaven at dawn; she asks Agni to master the enemy and to maintain the bond of husband and wife.
notes: Hymn-level paraphrase; a woman performing the offering as seer.

paraphrase: Your fixed ṛta is hidden by ṛta, Mitra and Varuṇa, where they unyoke the horses of the Sun; a thousand stood together there — that One; I saw the fairest of the gods' forms.
notes: Seer: Śrutavid Ātreya (checked).

paraphrase: The inspired ones of the great inspired one yoke their mind (manas) and yoke their thoughts (dhī); he alone, knowing the ways, has ordained the priestly offices — great is the praise of the god Savitṛ.

paraphrase: I proclaim this great māyā of the famous asura Varuṇa, who, standing in the atmosphere, measured out the earth with the sun as with a measuring rod.

A fixed light (jyotis) is set to be seen; mind is the swiftest among flying things; all the gods, of one mind and one intent, go toward the one will (kratu).
notes: Deity: Agni Vaiśvānara (checked).

You, Agni, Atharvan churned forth from the lotus, from the head of every priest.
He became the counter-form of every form; that form of his is to be seen; Indra goes in many forms by his māyās; his thousand bay horses are yoked.

paraphrase: Vasiṣṭha is addressed: you are the son of Mitra and Varuṇa, born, O brahman, from the mind of Urvaśī; the drop that fell by divine formulation all the gods placed in the lotus.
Rudra with the strong bow and swift arrows, lord of all creatures on earth and in heaven, is asked to let his missile pass us by, to spare our children and to grant his thousand remedies.

paraphrase: We worship Tryambaka, the fragrant, the increaser of prosperity; like a cucumber from its stalk, may I be freed from death, not from immortality.

paraphrase: That bright eye set by the gods rises in front; may we see a hundred autumns, may we live a hundred autumns.

Vasiṣṭha speaks with himself: when shall I be inside Varuṇa? Will he enjoy my offering without anger? When shall I, gracious-minded, behold his mercy? I ask the knowing ones what the sin is; the sages all say the same: Varuṇa is angry with you. What was my chief sin, Varuṇa, that you would slay your friend and singer?
Release us from the wrongs of our fathers and from those we have done with our own bodies; release Vasiṣṭha as a thief who fed on cattle, as a calf from its tether.

It was not my own will (dakṣa), Varuṇa, but a seduction (dhruti): wine (surā), anger (manyu), dice, thoughtlessness (acitti); the elder is near in the younger's fault; even sleep does not ward off wrong (anṛta).

When Varuṇa and I boarded the boat and steered it to the middle of the sea, gliding over the waters' backs we rocked in a swing for joy; Varuṇa set Vasiṣṭha in the boat and by his powers made him a seer (ṛṣi), a singer in the fair days.
May Varuṇa, as we dwell in secure abodes, loosen the fetter (pāśa) from us; may we win the favour of Aditi's lap.
notes: The Anukramaṇī marks this verse as 'releasing from the fetter' (pāśavimocanī), checked.

paraphrase: Let me not go to the house of clay, King Varuṇa; have mercy, mighty lord, have mercy.
Whatever offence we humans commit against the divine race, whatever of your ordinances (dharma) we have broken through thoughtlessness (acitti), do not harm us for that sin, O god.
When one of the frogs repeats the speech of another, as a pupil repeats his teacher's, all their parts are as if in unison as they chatter in the waters.

paraphrase: May I die today if I am a sorcerer (yātudhāna) or if I have burnt away a man's life; then may he be severed from his ten heroes who falsely calls me 'sorcerer'.

paraphrase: We have drunk the soma, we have become immortal, we have gone to the light, we have found the gods; what can hostility do to us now, what the malice of a mortal, O immortal?

paraphrase: One Agni is kindled in many ways; one Sun pervades all; one Dawn shines over all this; the One has become all this.

paraphrase: Offer praise to Indra if he truly exists; 'there is no Indra', says Nema, 'who has seen him? whom shall we praise?' — 'Here I am, singer, look at me here; I surpass all beings in greatness; the directives of ṛta make me grow'.

paraphrase: When Speech, uttering what is not understood, sat down as queen of the gods, she milked out food and strength; the gods begot the goddess Speech, and animals of every form speak her; may she, the cow of speech, come to us well praised.
Flow, Soma, in the sweetest, most exhilarating stream, pressed for Indra to drink.
Whoever studies the purifying (pāvamānī) verses, the essence gathered by the seers, eats all his food purified, made sweet by Mātariśvan.
notes: A verse of the Soma book on the merit of reciting the Soma book itself.

paraphrase: Your filter is spread out, lord of sacred speech (brahmaṇaspati); as master you go round its limbs on every side; the raw one whose body is unheated (by tapas) does not attain it; only the cooked (śṛta) who bear it attain it.

Various are our thoughts and the callings of men: the carpenter seeks what is broken, the physician the injured, the brahman one who presses soma; 'I am a poet, my father a physician, my mother grinds grain' — with various thoughts we seek wealth; flow, Soma, for Indra.

paraphrase: Honour with oblation King Yama, son of Vivasvant, the gatherer of peoples, who went along the great heights and searched out the path for many.
Go forth, go forth by the ancient paths on which our fathers went before; you will see the two kings rejoicing in svadhā, Yama and god Varuṇa.
Unite with the fathers, with Yama, with your merit of sacrifices and gifts (iṣṭāpūrta) in the highest heaven; leaving fault behind, come home again; unite with a body, full of vigour.

Let the fathers rise up — the lower, the higher and the middle, worthy of soma — those who have gone to the life-breath (asu), gentle and knowing ṛta; may they help us at our calls.

paraphrase: Let your eye go to the sun, your breath (ātman) to the wind; go to heaven and to earth according to dharma, or go to the waters if that is your lot; settle in the plants with your limbs.

These women, not widowed, with good husbands, anointed with ghee as salve, may they enter; tearless, free of sickness, well adorned, let the wives first ascend the seat (yonim agre).

Do not play with dice; till your field; delight in what you have, thinking it much; there are your cows, gambler, there your wife — so the noble Savitṛ tells me.

Through the sacrifice they followed the track of speech; they found her entered into the seers; they brought her and distributed her in many places; the seven singers praise her together.
One who sees has not seen speech, one who hears does not hear her; but to another she opens her body as a loving, well-dressed wife to her husband.

When they divided the Person, into how many parts did they arrange him? What was his mouth, what his arms, what are his thighs and feet called? The brāhmaṇa was his mouth, his arms were made the rājanya, his thighs the vaiśya, from his feet the śūdra was born.

paraphrase: The wise see with the heart and mind the bird anointed with the asura's māyā; the seers look within the ocean; the disposers seek the track of its rays.

paraphrase: Ṛta and satya were born from kindled tapas; from that night was born, and from that the flowing ocean.

original.text: ṛtaṃ ca satyaṃ cābhīddhāt tapaso 'dhy ajāyata | tato rātry ajāyata tataḥ samudro arṇavaḥ
original.edition: Śākala Saṃhitā, standard text (IAST, accents omitted); wording checked against the Devanāgarī text in sources_raw/DharmicData

paraphrase: From the ocean the year was born, ordering days and nights, ruler over all that blinks; the Disposer (dhātṛ) fashioned sun and moon as before (yathāpūrvam), and heaven, earth, the atmosphere and the light.
notes: 'As before' (yathāpūrvam) is read by the later tradition as the recurrence of creations (interpretive).

paraphrase: Go together, speak together, let your minds know together, as the gods of old sat together at their share; common be your counsel, common your assembly, common your mind, your thought together; common be your intention, common your hearts, common your mind, that you may live well together.

original.text: saṃ gacchadhvaṃ saṃ vadadhvaṃ saṃ vo manāṃsi jānatām
original.edition: Śākala Saṃhitā, standard text (IAST, accents omitted); wording checked against the Devanāgarī text in sources_raw/DharmicData

paraphrase: Come, Agni, praised, to the feast, to the giving of oblations; sit as hotṛ on the sacred grass — the first verse of the Pūrvārcika (= Ṛgveda 6.16.10), the text of the first melody.

Homage to your wrath, Rudra, and to your arrow; homage to your bow and your two arms; with your most auspicious body, not terrible, not revealing evil (aghorā apāpakāśinī), look on us, mountain-dweller; the first divine physician has spoken for us; the blue-necked, red one who creeps away, whom cowherds and water-bearing women have seen and all beings see — may he, seen, be gracious to us; unstring your bow and turn your arrows away.

original.text: namas te rudra manyava uto ta iṣave namaḥ
original.edition: Taittirīya Saṃhitā, standard text (IAST, accents omitted); wording checked against sources_raw/raw_etexts

notes: = VS 16.1–14 in substance (VS 16.1 checked; TS 4.5.1 checked).

paraphrase: The litany of homage (namaḥ … namaḥ): to Rudra as lord of the quarters, trees, animals, paths, food and the well-nourished; as lord of thieves, robbers and forest-rangers; as present in hosts and their lords, in carpenters, chariot-makers, potters, smiths, hunters and dog-keepers; in the small and the great, the elder and the younger, the first-born and the last-born; in paths and streams, in pools and rains, in clouds and lightning, in grass, leaves and dust; as the blue-throated and the white-throated, the one with braided hair and the shaven, the one with a thousand eyes and a hundred quivers.
notes: Passage-level summary of anuvākas 2–9 from memory; the order of items is not reproduced.

paraphrase: Homage to Soma and to Rudra … homage to the source of happiness and the source of delight (śambhu, mayobhu), to the maker of happiness and the maker of delight (śaṅkara, mayaskara), to the auspicious and the more auspicious (namaḥ śivāya ca śivatarāya ca).

original.text: namaḥ śivāya ca śivatarāya ca
original.edition: Taittirīya Saṃhitā, standard text (IAST, accents omitted); wording checked against sources_raw/raw_etexts

notes: Checked in the local TS text. The Śaiva traditions take 'namaḥ śivāya' here as the Vedic source of the five-syllable mantra (brw:satarudriya-to-saiva). = VS 16.41.

paraphrase: The countless thousands of Rudras on the earth, in the atmosphere and in heaven, blue-necked and white-throated, in trees, in food, in drink, on the paths — their bows are unstrung a thousand leagues away; homage to them all, with ten (fingers) to each quarter; may they be gracious to us; whom we hate and who hates us we place in their jaws.
notes: Passage-level summary from memory; VS 16.54 checked.

paraphrase: The Camaka: 'food and impulse for me … in-breath, out-breath and diffused breath for me, life (asu), thought (citta), what is thought upon, speech, mind, eye, ear, skill, strength, vigour … truth and faith for me … the past and the future for me … ṛta and the immortal, freedom from sickness, long life, fearlessness for me … the soma-rites and their vessels for me … one, three, five … four, eight, twelve … for me' — each to be made fit by the sacrifice.
notes: Opening items checked in the local TS text; = VS 18.1–27.

paraphrase: In the Tryambaka offering, the Tryambaka verse ('we worship Tryambaka … may I be freed from death, not from immortality') is followed by: 'this is your share, Rudra; with this provision go beyond the Mūjavants, your bow unstrung, Pināka in hand, clad in skin'.
notes: Checked in the local TS text (1.8, near kaṇḍikā 11); the anuvāka number 6 is from memory. The Tryambaka offerings belong to the Sākamedha of the seasonal rites (moderate).

paraphrase: The first formula of the White Yajurveda: (you twigs) for food, for strength; you are winds; may god Savitṛ impel you to the best of works; swell, inviolable cows, with Indra's share, rich in offspring, free from sickness and consumption; let no thief rule over you.
Agni, lord of vows, I shall undertake the vow; may I be able to do it; may it succeed for me; here I go from untruth to truth.

original.text: agne vratapate vrataṃ cariṣyāmi tac chakeyaṃ tan me rādhyatām | idam aham anṛtāt satyam upaimi
original.edition: Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā (Mādhyandina), standard text (IAST, accents omitted); wording checked against sources_raw/DharmicData

paraphrase: Two forms of the Tryambaka verse: 'may I be freed from death, not from immortality', and, with 'finder of husbands' (pativedanam), 'may I be freed from here (the father's house), not from there'; followed (3.61) by sending Rudra with his provision beyond the Mūjavants, bow unstrung, clad in skin, auspicious (śiva).
notes: Checked in the local VS text.

paraphrase: The threefold life-span of Jamadagni, the threefold life-span of Kaśyapa, the threefold life-span that is among the gods — may that threefold life-span (tryāyuṣa) be ours.
notes: Checked in the local VS text. Its later use in rites of tonsure and with the application of ash is recalled from memory (not recorded as teaching).

paraphrase: At the start of building the fire altar: Savitṛ, first yoking the mind (manas) and stretching out the thoughts (dhī) for truth (tattva), discerned the light of Agni and brought it from the earth; with yoked mind we are in the impulse of the god Savitṛ for strength to reach heaven; the inspired yoke their mind and their thoughts; 'I yoke with homage your ancient prayer'.
notes: VS 11.1 checked ('yuñjānaḥ prathamaṃ manas tattvāya savitā dhiyaḥ'); = TS 4.1.1. The Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad (2.1–5) quotes these verses at the head of its yoga chapter.

paraphrase: Homage to the hosts (gaṇa) and to the lords of hosts (gaṇapati), to the troops (vrāta) and their lords, to the skilled and their lords, to those of varied form and of every form.
notes: Checked in the local VS text.

paraphrase: The countless thousands of Rudras upon the earth — their bows we unstring a thousand leagues away.
notes: Kautsa cites this verse against 'Rudra stood alone, there was no second' (TS 1.8.6) as an instance of mantras stating opposed things (vipratiṣiddha); Yāska answers (Nirukta 1.15–16).

paraphrase: The opening of the Camaka in the White Yajurveda: 'food and impulse for me, effort and exertion, thought and will, sound and verse, hearing and learning …'.

May a brāhmaṇa be born in the realm radiant with sacred knowledge; a rājanya, a hero, an archer, a great charioteer; a milch-cow, a draught-ox, a swift horse, a skilful woman, a victorious warrior, a youth fit for the assembly; may the rain fall when we wish; may our plants ripen; may we have security and prosperity.
notes: Checked (opening); prayer of the horse sacrifice.

paraphrase: Riddle-exchange (brahmodya) of the horse sacrifice: 'Who moves alone? Who is born again? What is the remedy for cold? What is the great field?' — 'The sun moves alone; the moon is born again; fire is the remedy for cold; the earth is the great field'; and further questions and answers.
notes: VS 23.9–10 checked; the range of the whole exchange from memory.

paraphrase: As I speak this auspicious speech to the people — to brahmin and rājanya, to śūdra and ārya, to one's own and to the stranger — may I be dear to the gods and to the giver of gifts here.
notes: Checked. Dayānanda Sarasvatī cited this verse for the right of all to hear the Veda (recent reading).

paraphrase: The Puruṣa hymn as recited in the White Yajurveda (31.1–16), with minor differences from RV 10.90 (e.g. 'covering the earth all round').
I know this great Person, sun-coloured, beyond darkness; only by knowing him does one go beyond death; there is no other path for going.

original.text: vedāham etaṃ puruṣaṃ mahāntam ādityavarṇaṃ tamasaḥ parastāt | tam eva viditvāti mṛtyum eti nānyaḥ panthā vidyate 'yanāya
original.edition: Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā (Mādhyandina), standard text (IAST, accents omitted); wording checked against sources_raw/DharmicData

notes: One of the six 'Uttaranārāyaṇa' verses (31.17–22); also Śvetāśvatara 3.8 (reference only).

paraphrase: Prajāpati moves within the womb; unborn, he is born in many ways; the wise see his source; in him all the worlds stand.
That indeed is Agni, that the Sun, that Wind, that the Moon; that is the bright, that is brahman, those the waters, he Prajāpati.
There is no likeness (pratimā) of him whose name is great glory.

original.text: na tasya pratimā asti yasya nāma mahad yaśaḥ
original.edition: Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā (Mādhyandina), standard text (IAST, accents omitted); wording checked against sources_raw/DharmicData

notes: Followed by pratīkas of 'Hiraṇyagarbha…', 'may he not harm me…' (checked). Also Śvetāśvatara 4.19 (reference only).

paraphrase: Vena saw that highest, hidden in secret (guhā), in which all becomes one nest; into it all this enters and from it comes forth; he is woven warp and woof through creatures, all-pervading.
That divine (mind) which goes far away from one who is awake and likewise returns to one asleep, far-going, the one light of lights — may that mind of mine be of auspicious resolve (śivasaṅkalpa).

original.text: yaj jāgrato dūram udaiti daivaṃ tad u suptasya tathaivaiti | dūraṃgamaṃ jyotiṣāṃ jyotir ekaṃ tan me manaḥ śivasaṅkalpam astu
original.edition: Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā (Mādhyandina), standard text (IAST, accents omitted); wording checked against sources_raw/DharmicData

paraphrase: That by which the wise and skilful do their works in the sacrifice and in the assemblies, the unprecedented wonder (yakṣa) within creatures — may that mind of mine be of auspicious resolve.

That which is knowing (prajñāna), thought (cetas) and steadfastness (dhṛti), the immortal light within creatures, without which no act whatever is done — may that mind of mine be of auspicious resolve.
That immortal by which all this — past, present and future — is held, by which the sacrifice of seven hotṛs is spread — may that mind of mine be of auspicious resolve.

That in which the verses, the chants and the formulas are fixed like spokes in the nave of a chariot, in which all the thought (citta) of creatures is woven — may that mind of mine be of auspicious resolve.
That which leads men as a good charioteer guides horses with the reins, heart-seated, ageless, swiftest — may that mind of mine be of auspicious resolve.
notes: The charioteer image may be compared with the Kaṭha Upaniṣad's chariot (1.3.3–9) — comparison is interpretive.

paraphrase: I take refuge in the ṛc as speech, in the yajus as mind, in the sāman as breath; I take refuge in eye and ear; speech, vigour, strength and in-breath and out-breath be in me.
notes: Checked (opening).

paraphrase: Bhūḥ, bhuvaḥ, svaḥ — the Gāyatrī ('we meditate on that excellent radiance of the god Savitṛ; may he impel our thoughts') recited with the three utterances (vyāhṛti).
notes: Checked in the local VS text.

paraphrase: Peace (śānti) be heaven, peace the atmosphere, peace the earth, peace the waters, peace the plants, peace the trees, peace the All-gods, peace brahman, peace everything; peace, only peace — may that peace be mine.
notes: Checked.

paraphrase: May all beings look on me with the eye of a friend (mitra); may I look on all beings with the eye of a friend; may we look on one another with the eye of a friend.

original.text: mitrasya mā cakṣuṣā sarvāṇi bhūtāni samīkṣantām | mitrasyāhaṃ cakṣuṣā sarvāṇi bhūtāni samīkṣe | mitrasya cakṣuṣā samīkṣāmahe
original.edition: Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā (Mādhyandina), standard text (IAST, accents omitted); wording checked against sources_raw/DharmicData

paraphrase: That bright eye set by the gods rises in front: may we see a hundred autumns, live a hundred autumns, hear a hundred autumns, speak a hundred autumns, be undiminished a hundred autumns, and more than a hundred autumns.

At the close of the Mādhyandina Saṃhitā: 'Oṃ, intent (kratu), remember; remember what was done'; 'Agni, lead us by the good path'; 'the face of truth is covered with a golden vessel; the Person who is in the sun, he am I; Oṃ, the void (kha) is brahman'.
notes: Checked in the local VS text. VS 40 is the Mādhyandina form of the Īśa Upaniṣad (U03 owns src:isa-upanisad); recorded here for its Saṃhitā wording.

paraphrase: May Vācaspati, lord of speech, place in me today the strengths and bodies of the thrice-seven who go about bearing all forms.
notes: Header: 'medhājananam' (production of retentive wisdom), seer Atharvan (checked); traditionally recited at the start of Vedic study (moderate).

paraphrase: Let your heart-burning and jaundice go up to the sun; we wrap you in the colour of the red bull for long life, that this man be free of defect and no longer yellow; we place your yellowness in parrots and thrushes.
notes: Checked (header: heart-disease and jaundice).

paraphrase: The night-born dark plant (rāmā, kṛṣṇā, asiknī) is asked to colour away the white leprosy (kilāsa) and grey spots, to let the patient's own colour return; the white mark born of bone, of body and of skin, made by a hostile spell, is destroyed.
notes: 1.23 checked.

paraphrase: Vena saw that highest, hidden in secret, in which all becomes one form; from it the dappled cow milked those being born; the light-finding throngs shouted to it.
notes: Header: 'paramaṃ dhāma', deity brahman, ātman (checked). 2.1.3 repeats 'the one name-giver of the gods' (cf. RV 10.82.3).

paraphrase: Charm against worms (krimi): the rising sun is asked to slay the worms, visible and invisible, in the body; they are crushed as with a stone.
notes: Header checked (krimināśanam, seer Kaṇva); content paraphrased at hymn level from memory.

paraphrase: Charm against the inherited disease (kṣetriya) and consumption (yakṣma) with the horn of the swift deer, the two stars called 'the Unfasteners', and the waters.
notes: Header checked (deities: the deer, the two stars, the waters, yakṣma-destroying); content from memory.

paraphrase: I make you of one heart and one mind, free from hatred; love one another as a cow loves her new-born calf; let the son be devoted to the father, of one mind with the mother; let the wife speak honeyed, gentle words to the husband; let not brother hate brother nor sister sister; united, of one purpose, speak with auspicious speech.

original.text: sahṛdayaṃ sāṃmanasyam avidveṣaṃ kṛṇomi vaḥ | anyo anyam abhi haryata vatsaṃ jātam ivāghnyā
original.edition: Śaunaka Saṃhitā, standard text (IAST, accents omitted); wording checked against the Devanāgarī text in sources_raw/DharmicData

paraphrase: Whoever stands, walks, sneaks, goes secretly or furtively — when two sit together and plot, King Varuṇa, the third, knows it; this earth and that far heaven are King Varuṇa's, the two oceans his belly; one who crept beyond the sky would not escape; his spies with a thousand eyes look over the earth; he has counted the blinkings of men; Varuṇa's seven-by-seven fetters, threefold, are to bind the one who speaks untruth and release the one who speaks truth.
notes: Header: 'satyānṛtasamīkṣakaḥ' (Varuṇa, examiner of truth and untruth), checked.

paraphrase: Charm against fever (takman): Agni is asked to drive the fever away; the fever that makes men yellow, that comes every third day or in autumn, is sent off to distant peoples.
notes: Header checked (takmanāśanam, Bhṛgvaṅgiras); content summary from memory.

paraphrase: You who are neither alive nor dead, immortal child of the gods, Sleep (svapna): Varuṇānī is your mother, Yama your father; we know your birth — you are Yama's instrument, the ender, death; protect us from bad dreaming.
notes: Checked (header: duḥṣvapnanāśanam).

paraphrase: Medhā (retentive wisdom), come to us first with cows and horses and the rays of the sun; I invoke the first medhā, full of brahman, impelled by brahman, praised by the seers, drunk by the brahmacārins, for the favour of the gods.
notes: Checked (header: medhāvardhanam, seer Śaunaka).

paraphrase: Charm for long life: homage to the ender, to death; let the in-breaths and out-breaths stay here; let this man be here with his life-breath in the portion of the sun, in the world of immortality; we lift you with divine speech from the fetters of Nirṛti; step up from here, man, freeing yourself from death's fetter; do not be cut off from this world, from the sight of Agni and the sun; let not your mind go there; do not follow the fathers; do not brood on those who are gone; do not go on that path — ahead is fear, here with you is no fear.
notes: Checked (verses 1–10).

paraphrase: Virāj was in the beginning all this; she went up and entered the householder's fire, the offering fire, the southern fire, the assembly (sabhā), the council (samiti) and the consultation; whoever knows this becomes a householder, dear to the gods, worthy of the sacrificial fee, fit for assembly and council; gods, men, asuras, fathers, serpents and others milked from her their several foods.
notes: First paryāya checked; the milkings in the later paryāyas from memory.

paraphrase: Hospitality is the sacrifice: the host who looks upon his guests beholds the place of sacrifice; greeting them is undertaking consecration (dīkṣā); the water he offers is the sacrificial water; the couches and cushions are the enclosing sticks, the food the oblation; so honouring a guest is equal to performing the sacrifice.
notes: Checked (opening paryāya; header 'atithi-satkāra').

paraphrase: By Brahman one attains the learned (śrotriya), this Parameṣṭhin, this Agni; Brahman measured the year; Brahman dwells in the gods and the divine folk; Brahman is the kṣatra; by Brahman the earth was set out, heaven placed above, and the atmosphere spread across.
notes: Checked (questions 'by whom…?' answered 'by brahman').

paraphrase: Atharvan sewed together his head and his heart; from the brain, above, the purifier (pavamāna) drove upward from the head.
notes: Checked. 10.2.27: 'that head of Atharvan is a sealed treasure-chest of the gods; breath, food and mind guard it' (checked).

paraphrase: He who knows the stronghold (pur) of Brahman, from which the person is called puruṣa, enveloped with immortality — to him Brahman and the Brāhmas gave sight, breath and offspring; sight and breath do not leave him before old age.
Eight-wheeled, nine-gated is the unconquerable stronghold of the gods; in it is a golden sheath (kośa), heavenly, covered with light.
notes: Checked. 'Eight wheels' (aṣṭācakra) is later read by some as the body's centres (cakras) — an interpretive reading not stated in the verse.

paraphrase: In that golden sheath, three-spoked, resting on three supports, the self-possessed wonder (yakṣam ātmanvat) — that the knowers of Brahman know; into the radiant, golden, unconquered stronghold Brahman entered.
In which limb of him does tapas abide, in which is ṛta set, where is the vow (vrata), where faith (śraddhā), in which limb is truth (satya) established? — the questions to Skambha.
notes: Checked; deity Skambha or Ātman.

paraphrase: Those who know Brahman in man (puruṣa) know the Supreme (parameṣṭhin); who knows the Supreme and who knows Prajāpati, who know the highest Brahman (jyeṣṭha brahman), they know Skambha.

Homage to that highest Brahman whose foot (measure) is the earth, whose belly the atmosphere, who made heaven his head; whose eye is the sun and the moon renewed again, who made Agni his mouth; whose in-breath and out-breath are the wind, whose eyes the Aṅgirases, who made the quarters his senses.
notes: 10.7.32 checked; 33–34 from memory.

paraphrase: Homage to that highest Brahman who presides over what has been and what will be and over all, whose alone is the light (svar).
notes: Checked; seer Kutsa, deity Ātman.

paraphrase: You are woman, you are man, you are the boy and the maiden too; you, old, totter with a staff; born, you face in every direction; … one god has entered the mind; the first-born, he is within the womb.
notes: Checked. Parallel in Śvetāśvatara 4.3 (reference only).

paraphrase: From the full the full is drawn up; the full is sprinkled with the full; may we know today whence it is sprinkled.
notes: Checked. Compare the Bṛhadāraṇyaka's 'pūrṇam adaḥ pūrṇam idam' (5.1.1), reference only.

paraphrase: The lotus with nine gates, covered with three strands (guṇa) — the self-possessed wonder (yakṣa) that is in it, that the knowers of Brahman know.
notes: Checked. 'Three guṇas' here are 'strands'; their identification with the three qualities of Sāṃkhya is a later reading (logged as a contested equivalence).

paraphrase: Free from desire, wise, immortal, self-existent, satisfied with the essence, lacking in nothing — knowing him, the wise, ageless, youthful self (ātman), one does not fear death.

original.text: akāmo dhīro amṛtaḥ svayaṃbhū rasena tṛpto na kutaś canonaḥ | tam eva vidvān na bibhāya mṛtyor ātmānaṃ dhīram ajaraṃ yuvānam
original.edition: Śaunaka Saṃhitā, standard text (IAST, accents omitted); wording checked against the Devanāgarī text in sources_raw/DharmicData

paraphrase: Hymn to Bhava and Śarva (Rudra): the two lords of beings, lords of cattle (paśupati), are asked to be gracious, not to loose their arrow, not to harm biped or quadruped; homage to Rudra from every side, to his face, eyes, skin and limbs; the five kinds of animals — cows, horses, men, goats and sheep — are allotted to Paśupati.
notes: Checked (verses 1–9).

paraphrase: Homage to Prāṇa, in whose control is all this, who has become the lord of all, in whom all is established.

original.text: prāṇāya namo yasya sarvam idaṃ vaśe | yo bhūtaḥ sarvasyeśvaro yasmin sarvaṃ pratiṣṭhitam
original.edition: Śaunaka Saṃhitā, standard text (IAST, accents omitted); wording checked against the Devanāgarī text in sources_raw/DharmicData

paraphrase: Prāṇa clothes creatures as a father his dear son; Prāṇa is lord of all, of what breathes and what does not; Prāṇa is death, Prāṇa is fever; the gods revere Prāṇa; Prāṇa sets the truth-speaker in the highest world.
The swan (haṃsa), rising from the waters, does not lift one foot; if he were to lift it, there would be neither today nor tomorrow, neither night nor day, and it would never dawn.
The eight-wheeled, one-felly (wheel) turns, with a thousand syllables, forward in front, back behind; with half it produced the whole world — what is the sign of its other half?
Upright among sleepers it keeps awake; it never lies down sideways; no one has heard of its sleeping among the sleepers.
Prāṇa, do not turn away from me; you shall not be other than me; like the embryo of the waters I bind you to me, Prāṇa, that I may live.
The Vedic student (brahmacārin) goes about quickening both worlds; in him the gods become of one mind; he upholds earth and heaven; he fills his teacher with tapas.
The teacher, initiating (upanayamāna) the student, makes him an embryo within; he carries him three nights in his belly; when he is born the gods gather to see him.

This fuel is the earth, the second the sky; he fills the atmosphere with fuel; with fuel, girdle, toil (śrama) and tapas the student fills the worlds; born before brahman, clothed in heat, he rose up by tapas; from him were born the brāhmaṇa, the highest brahman and all the gods with immortality; kindled with fuel, clad in black antelope skin, consecrated (dīkṣita), long-bearded, he goes at once from the eastern to the northern ocean.

By brahmacarya and tapas the king protects the realm; by brahmacarya the teacher seeks a student; by brahmacarya a maiden wins a young husband; by brahmacarya the ox and the horse win their fodder; by brahmacarya and tapas the gods struck down death; by brahmacarya Indra brought the light to the gods.
In the Remainder (ucchiṣṭa) are name and form (nāma-rūpa); in the Remainder the world is set; in the Remainder Indra and Agni, and the whole universe, are held together within.
Therefore the knower thinks of the person (puruṣa): 'this is brahman', for all the deities dwell in him as cows in a stall.
notes: Checked; the hymn (seer Kauru-pathi) tells how the gods entered the mortal body.

paraphrase: Great truth, strict order (ṛta), consecration (dīkṣā), austerity (tapas), sacred formulation (brahman) and sacrifice (yajña) uphold the earth; may she, mistress of what was and what will be, make wide room for us.

original.edition: Śaunaka Saṃhitā, standard text (IAST, accents omitted); wording checked against the Devanāgarī text in sources_raw/DharmicData

paraphrase: The Earth is my mother, I am the son of the Earth; Parjanya is the father — may he fill us.

original.text: mātā bhūmiḥ putro ahaṃ pṛthivyāḥ
original.edition: Śaunaka Saṃhitā, standard text (IAST, accents omitted); wording checked against the Devanāgarī text in sources_raw/DharmicData

paraphrase: What of you I dig out, Earth, may that quickly grow again; may I not strike your vitals (marman), O purifier, nor your heart.
Earth, bearing people of many speeches and of various dharmas according to their dwellings, is asked to yield a thousand streams of wealth like a steady cow.
He is the one, the one-alone (ekavṛt), the one only; in him these gods become one-alone.
notes: Checked (local edition 13.4.12–13); preceding verses identify him with Savitṛ, Dhātṛ, Vāyu, Aryaman, Varuṇa, Rudra, Mahādeva, Agni, Sūrya and Mahāyama.

paraphrase: Whoever knows this god as one-alone — he is called neither second nor third nor fourth, neither fifth nor sixth nor seventh, neither eighth nor ninth nor tenth.
notes: Whitney numbering; in the local edition these verses stand in the next sūkta (13.5.16–18), checked.

paraphrase: In the marriage rite: we worship Aryaman, good kinsman, finder of husbands; like a cucumber from its stalk I release (the bride) from here, not from there.
notes: Checked; the Atharvaveda's marriage form of the Tryambaka verse addresses Aryaman.

paraphrase: There was a Vrātya, moving; he stirred Prajāpati; Prajāpati saw gold in himself and brought it forth; it became one, it became the mark, the great, the eldest, brahman, tapas, truth; by it he was born; he grew, he became great, he became Mahādeva; he encompassed the lordship of the gods and became Īśāna; he became the sole Vrātya (ekavrātya); he took up a bow — Indra's bow (the rainbow) — its belly blue, its back red; with the blue he envelops the unfriendly rival, with the red he pierces the hater, say the expounders of brahman.
notes: Checked.

paraphrase: The Vrātya stood upright for a year; the gods asked 'Vrātya, why do you stand?'; he asked that a seat be brought; its legs were summer and spring, autumn and rains; its lengthwise boards the Bṛhat and Rathantara chants; its warp the verses, its woof the formulas; its covering the Veda, its cushion brahman; he mounted it.

When a Vrātya who knows this comes as guest to a king's house, the king should honour him as higher than himself, so he does not offend against the kṣatra or the realm; from him brahman and kṣatra arose; when such a Vrātya comes as guest to any house, the householder should rise and greet him and offer him water and food.
notes: 15.10.1–8 checked; 15.11–13 from memory.

paraphrase: Of that Vrātya there are seven in-breaths, seven out-breaths, seven diffused breaths; his first in-breath, called 'upward', is fire; the second, 'risen', the sun; the third, 'borne near', the moon; the fourth, 'pervading', the purifying wind; the fifth, 'womb', the waters; the sixth, 'dear', the animals; the seventh, 'unmeasured', these creatures; and so for his out-breaths and diffused breaths.
notes: 15.15 checked; 15.16–17 (out-breaths, diffused breaths) from memory.

paraphrase: Agni is asked to bring all the fathers to eat the oblation — those who were buried, those cast out, those burned and those exposed; those burned by fire and those not burned by fire who rejoice in the midst of heaven by svadhā.
notes: Checked.

paraphrase: This woman, choosing her husband's world, lies down beside you, the departed mortal, keeping the ancient dharma; grant her offspring and wealth here; rise, woman, to the world of the living; you lie beside one whose life is gone; come — you have become the wife of him who took your hand.
notes: Checked; 18.3.3 continues 'I saw a young woman being led, the living led around from the dead'.

paraphrase: Peaceful be heaven, peaceful the earth, peaceful the wide atmosphere, peaceful the waters and the plants; peaceful the forerunning signs, peaceful what is done and not done, what has been and what will be; this supreme goddess Speech, sharpened by brahman, by which the terrible was created — by that let there be peace for us.
notes: Checked.

paraphrase: Desiring the good, the light-finding seers first undertook tapas and consecration (dīkṣā); from that were born the kingdom, strength and vigour; let the gods bow to it for this one.
notes: Checked.

paraphrase: Desire (kāma) arose in the beginning, which was the first seed of mind; Kāma, of one origin with the great Kāma, give increase of wealth to the sacrificer.
notes: Checked.

paraphrase: Time (kāla) drives as a horse with seven reins, thousand-eyed, ageless, rich in seed; the inspired poets mount him; his wheels are all beings.
notes: Checked.

paraphrase: In Time is tapas, in Time the eldest, in Time brahman is gathered; Time is lord of all, who was the father of Prajāpati; by it this was impelled and born and in it established; Time, becoming brahman, bears the Supreme; Time created creatures, Time in the beginning Prajāpati; self-born Kaśyapa and tapas were born from Time.
notes: Checked.

paraphrase: From Time the waters came into being, and brahman, tapas and the quarters; by Time the sun rises and in Time sets again; by Time the wind blows, by Time the great earth stands; Time begot what was and what will be; from Time the verses (ṛc) arose and the formulas (yajus).
notes: Checked.

paraphrase: Kautsa's objection: if mantras serve to convey meaning, (study of the science of meaning) is needed — but 'the mantras are meaningless' (anarthakā hi mantrāḥ): their words and order are fixed; their form is already prescribed by the Brāhmaṇa; their meaning is impossible ('O plant, protect him'; 'O axe, do not hurt him', said while striking); they state opposed things (vipratiṣiddha) ('Rudra stood alone, there was no second' against 'countless thousands of Rudras'); they address one who already knows; they say 'Aditi is all'.
speaker: Kautsa (as reported by Yāska)

original.text: anarthakā hi mantrāḥ
original.edition: Nirukta (DCS text)

notes: Checked against the DCS Nirukta (1.15). Kautsa's view survives only in Yāska's report.

paraphrase: Yāska's reply: the mantras are meaningful because their words are the same as in ordinary speech; the Brāhmaṇa itself says a rite is perfect when the verse or formula describes the act being done; fixed word-order and apparently opposed statements occur in ordinary speech too; non-injury is understood from the scriptural statement; obscurity is not the post's fault if the blind man does not see it — it is the person's fault.

original.text: naiṣa sthāṇor aparādho yad enam andho na paśyati
original.edition: Nirukta (DCS text)

notes: Checked (DCS 1.16).

paraphrase: A mere post, a bearer of burdens, is he who has studied the Veda but does not understand its meaning; one who knows the meaning attains all good and, his sins shaken off by knowledge, goes to heaven; what is learned without understanding and merely repeated never blazes, like dry fuel without fire.

original.text: sthāṇur ayaṃ bhārahāraḥ kilābhūd adhītya vedaṃ na vijānāti yo 'rtham
original.edition: Nirukta (DCS text)

notes: Checked (DCS 1.18). A verse Yāska quotes.

paraphrase: The seers had direct perception of dharma (sākṣātkṛtadharmāṇaḥ); they handed on the mantras by instruction to later ones who lacked it; those later ones, weary of instruction, compiled this text — the Veda and the Vedāṅgas — for ease of grasping; the meaning is the flower and fruit of speech.

original.text: sākṣātkṛtadharmāṇa ṛṣayo babhūvuḥ
original.edition: Nirukta (DCS text)

notes: Checked (DCS 1.20).

paraphrase: On RV 1.164.32 ('having many offspring he has entered Nirṛti'): the wandering ascetics (parivrājakāḥ) say 'one with many births comes to misery'; the etymologists (nairuktāḥ) say it refers to the action of rain — the cloud, with many offspring, reaches the earth.

original.text: bahuprajāḥ kṛcchram āpadyata iti parivrājakāḥ | varṣakarmeti nairuktāḥ
original.edition: Nirukta (DCS text)

notes: Checked (DCS 2.8).

paraphrase: A seer (ṛṣi) is so called from 'seeing': 'he saw the hymns' (stomān dadarśa), says Aupamanyava.
notes: Section number from memory (low-moderate): not found in the DCS portion of chapter 2; wording 'ṛṣir darśanāt' well known.

paraphrase: Because of the deity's great majesty, the one Self (eka ātmā) is praised in many ways; the other gods are the limbs of the one Self.
notes: Ref confirmed via a citation 'Nirukta 7.4' in a local secondary text; wording recalled: 'mahābhāgyād devatāyā eka ātmā bahudhā stūyate; ekasyātmano 'nye devāḥ pratyaṅgāni bhavanti'.

paraphrase: The etymologists hold that there are only three deities: Agni, whose place is the earth; Vāyu or Indra, whose place is the atmosphere; and Sūrya, whose place is heaven — the many names belong to these by their greatness and differing functions.
notes: Section number from memory.

paraphrase: On the form of the gods: some say they are like persons (puruṣavidha), since they are praised and addressed as sentient beings with limbs and possessions; others say they are not like persons, since what is seen of them — fire, wind, sun, earth, moon — is not; or they may be of both kinds.
notes: Section numbers and wording recalled from memory (moderate).

paraphrase: Which are the four quarters of speech (RV 1.164.45)? Oṃ and the three great utterances, say the seers' school; noun, verb, preposition and particle, say the grammarians; mantra, ritual text, brāhmaṇa and ordinary speech as fourth, say the ritualists; ṛc, yajus, sāman and ordinary speech, say the etymologists; others name the speech of serpents, of birds, of small creeping things and ordinary speech; the teachers of the self name speech in animals, in instruments, in wild beasts and in the self.
notes: In the Nirukta's supplementary (pariśiṣṭa) chapters; section number and the exact list recalled from memory — LOW confidence, check first.

paraphrase: Seeing the decline of beings in each age, Vyāsa, for the continuity of the sacrifice performed by the four priests, divided the one Veda into four — Ṛg, Yajus, Sāma and Atharva — with Itihāsa-Purāṇa called the fifth Veda; Paila held the Ṛgveda, Jaimini sang the Sāman, Vaiśampāyana alone mastered the Yajus, Sumantu the Atharvāṅgirasas, Romaharṣaṇa the Itihāsa-Purāṇas; they in turn divided their Vedas through pupils and pupils' pupils, and the Vedas became branched (śākhin).
notes: Checked against the local Bhāgavata text (1.4.19–24).

paraphrase: The triple Veda is not within hearing of women, śūdras and inferior twice-born (dvijabandhu); for the good of those deluded about right action, the sage in compassion composed the story of the Bhārata.

original.text: strīśūdradvijabandhūnāṃ trayī na śrutigocarā
original.edition: Bhāgavata Purāṇa (local text)

notes: Checked.

paraphrase: Vaiśampāyana made twenty-seven branches of the Yajurveda tree and gave them to his pupils; when he incurred the sin of killing a brahmin by breaking the sages' compact, Yājñavalkya offered to perform the expiation alone, disparaging the others; the angry teacher bade him give back what he had learned; Yājñavalkya vomited the Yajus stained with blood, and the other pupils, becoming partridges (tittiri), took them up — hence they are Taittirīyas; those who performed the expiation were called Caraka-adhvaryus.
notes: Checked against the local Viṣṇu Purāṇa text (3.5.1–14).

paraphrase: Yājñavalkya, devoted to breath-control, praised the Sun as the door of liberation and the abode of the three Vedas; the Sun, taking the form of a horse (vājin), granted him Yajus unknown to his teacher, called 'unused' (ayātayāma); those who study them are called Vājins; their branches are fifteen, the Kāṇva and others.

The women who spoke brahman (brahmavādinī) in the Ṛgveda are named: Ghoṣā, Godhā, Viśvavārā, Apālā, Upaniṣad, Niṣad, Juhū Brahmajāyā, Agastya's sister, Aditi; Indrāṇī and Indra's mother, Saramā, Romaśā, Urvaśī, Lopāmudrā, the Rivers, Yamī, the wife (Śaśvatī); Śrī, Lākṣā, Sārparājñī, Vāc, Śraddhā, Medhā, Dakṣiṇā, Rātrī and Sūryā Sāvitrī.
notes: List and verse numbers recalled from memory (LOW); the Bṛhaddevatā text was not available locally. Check first.

paraphrase: The first (note) of the Sāman singers is the flute's madhyama; the second is gāndhāra, the third ṛṣabha, the fourth ṣaḍja, the fifth dhaivata, the sixth niṣāda, the seventh pañcama.

original.text: yaḥ sāmagānāṃ prathamaḥ sa veṇor madhyamaḥ svaraḥ
original.edition: Nāradīya Śikṣā (local text)

notes: Checked (1.5.1–2).

paraphrase: The peacock sounds ṣaḍja, cows low ṛṣabha, goats and sheep gāndhāra, the krauñca bird madhyama, the cuckoo in the flowering season pañcama, the horse dhaivata, the elephant niṣāda.
notes: Checked.

paraphrase: The places of the Sāman notes: kruṣṭa at the head, prathama on the forehead, dvitīya between the brows, tṛtīya at the ears, caturtha in the throat, mandra in the chest, atisvārya in the heart; on the hand the kruṣṭa is shown at the top of the thumb, prathama on the thumb, gāndhāra (dvitīya) on the forefinger, then the others on the following fingers.
notes: Checked (1.7.1–4).

paraphrase: Six are the worst reciters: the one who sings, the hasty, the head-shaker, the one who recites from writing, the one ignorant of the meaning, the weak-voiced; six are the virtues of a reciter: sweetness, distinct letters, right word-division, good accent, composure and command of tempo.
notes: Checked (verses 32–33).

paraphrase: A mantra deficient in accent or letter, wrongly applied, does not convey its meaning; that verbal thunderbolt harms the sacrificer, as 'Indra-śatru' did through a fault of accent.
notes: Checked (verse 52). The Indra-śatru story (Tvaṣṭṛ's mis-accented formula) is told in the Brāhmaṇas.

paraphrase: One who studies without the hand (gestures), lacking accent and letters, is burned by the Ṛg, Yajus and Sāman and goes to a lower birth; one who studies the Veda with the hand, with accent, letters and meaning, is purified by them and is honoured in the world of Brahman.
notes: Checked (verses 54–55).

paraphrase: The Veda is that text which makes known the supernatural means (alaukika upāya) of obtaining the desired and avoiding the undesired; it is authoritative in itself, being authorless.
notes: Paraphrase of the definition in Sāyaṇa's introductions (recalled; the same definition appears in his introduction to the Taittirīya Saṃhitā). Locator 'upodghāta' is chapter-level.

paraphrase: The seers at a sacrificial session on the Sarasvatī drove away Kavaṣa Ailūṣa as the son of a slave woman, unfit to drink with them; in the desert he saw the hymn to the Child of the Waters, the waters followed him, and the seers, knowing that the gods knew him, called him back.
notes: Section number and narrative recalled from memory (LOW). U02 owns the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa.
